fields.foundation: The Umayyad Caliphate was established in 661 CE after the assassination of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth of the Rashidun caliphs and the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, the long-serving governor of Syria and the most powerful figure in the Islamic world, then secured recognition as caliph. He made Damascus the seat of the caliphate in place of Ali's base at Kufa and the earlier capital of Medina. Muawiyah belonged to the Umayyad clan of the Quraysh, the clan that had led Meccan opposition to Muhammad until the Prophet's conquest of Mecca in 630. With his accession the caliphate ceased to be a leadership chosen by consultation and became a hereditary monarchy based in Syria. His nomination of his son Yazid as successor led directly to the Second Fitna (civil war, 680–692). During it Husayn ibn Ali, Ali's son and Muhammad's grandson, was killed with a small band of followers at Karbala in 680 by forces sent by Yazid's governor of Iraq, Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad. Karbala became the defining martyrdom of Shia Islam and deepened the division between what would become the Sunni and Shia traditions. The Marwanid branch of the dynasty was founded by Marwan I (r. 684–685). Under Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705) it recovered the caliphate from the rival Zubayrid claimant Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and it proved more stable and more inventive in administration than Muawiyah's line. Abd al-Malik also built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed around 691. The Great Mosque of Damascus was built in the reign of his son al-Walid I (r. 705–715). Under these two caliphs the caliphate expanded into Spain, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent at the same time, among the fastest territorial expansions in history.
fields.socioeconomy: The Umayyad economy rested on the agricultural surpluses of Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia, among the most productive farming regions of the ancient world. To these were added the revenues of trade between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean. At first the caliphate ran separate Byzantine and Sasanian administrative and monetary systems in the former territories of each. Abd al-Malik replaced this inherited practice with a single Islamic system. His coinage reform of the 690s ended with the aniconic gold dinar of 697, which abandoned Byzantine and Sasanian imagery in favour of Quranic inscriptions in Arabic. It gave the empire one currency and asserted Islamic authority over commerce. The jizya poll tax on non-Muslim subjects (dhimmis) and the kharaj land tax were the main sources of revenue. This created a lasting difficulty, because conversion reduced the population liable to jizya. Some governors, among them al-Hajjaj in Iraq, continued to tax converts or sent them back to the land. The pious caliph Umar II (r. 717–720) attempted to relieve converts of these burdens, but the problem persisted to the end of the dynasty. Arab tribal elites, above all those of Syria, gained most from the Umayyad system. Arab warriors drew stipends registered in the diwan, while the conquered lands were taxed through existing administrative structures with little disruption to production. Mediterranean trade in grain, oil, textiles, papyrus and luxury goods continued much as it had under Byzantine rule, with Arab merchants increasingly active alongside Greek, Coptic, Syrian Christian and Jewish commercial networks.
fields.military: The armies of the early caliphate were the most expansionist force of the seventh and early eighth centuries. Their conquests rivalled the campaigns of Alexander the Great in pace and scale and lasted far longer. The decisive early victories belonged to the Rashidun period that preceded the dynasty. At the Yarmuk in 636 Arab forces destroyed the Byzantine army defending Syria, and at al-Qadisiyya around 636–637 they broke the Sasanian army in Iraq. These battles opened the heartlands of two ancient empires that had exhausted one another in decades of warfare. Muawiyah himself had taken a leading part in these conquests as governor of Syria, where he built the first Arab war fleet, raided Cyprus and Rhodes, and defeated the Byzantine navy at the Battle of the Masts in 654 or 655. The Umayyads carried the conquests in both directions at once. In the west, Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan around 670 and North Africa was subdued. In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into Spain, beginning the Umayyad conquest of Hispania and overthrowing the Visigothic kingdom. Raids beyond the Pyrenees were checked by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours (Poitiers) in 732. In the east, Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Bukhara and Samarkand in Transoxiana, and Muhammad ibn Qasim led the Umayyad conquest of Sind in 711–712. The First Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s failed, as did a second siege in 717–718. Arab ships and siege methods could not overcome the city's strong walls or the devastating effect of Greek fire. Defeats at the hands of the Khazars in the Caucasus in 730 and the Turgesh in Central Asia marked further limits of expansion.
fields.governance: Umayyad government was an Arab tribal elite's attempt to administer an empire of many peoples, religions and languages. The elite did so by adapting what it found, without redesigning government as a whole. The Byzantine administrative framework in Syria, Palestine and Egypt was largely preserved. Greek-speaking officials continued to manage taxation, records and local government until Abd al-Malik's arabisation reforms of the late 690s made Arabic the language of the central registers. In Iraq and Persia, Sasanian administrative traditions were likewise maintained through existing personnel. The dihqans, the Persian landed gentry, continued to collect taxes from village communities, until the Persian-language registers were also arabised. Governing through existing institutions while asserting Muslim political supremacy reduced disruption, but it produced a state identified more with Arab rule than with Islam as a universal community. Arabs were privileged over non-Arab Muslims (mawali) in military stipends, appointments and social status. No other choice of the dynasty had greater political consequences: it generated deep resentment among Persian, Berber and other converts, which the Abbasid Revolution would later mobilise. Provincial government was entrusted to powerful governors, such as al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who ruled Iraq and the east from 694 to 714 with notorious severity. Islamic law was administered by appointed judges (qadis), though customary and pre-Islamic legal traditions continued to govern much of daily life among non-Arab and non-Muslim communities. The court at Damascus, together with the desert palaces such as Qusayr Amra, adopted elements of Byzantine and Persian royal display, which pious critics condemned as incompatible with the egalitarian ideals of early Islam.
fields.impact: Within less than a century the Umayyad Caliphate changed the religious, linguistic and cultural geography of three continents. The Arab conquests ended Byzantine rule in the Levant, Egypt and North Africa and destroyed the Sasanian Empire. These lands began to turn into predominantly Arabic-speaking and, in the end, Muslim societies, a change that proved irreversible across most of the conquered territory. Conversion, however, was gradual: in Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Persia, long centres of Christianity and Zoroastrianism, Muslims probably became a majority only over the following centuries, and substantial Christian and Jewish communities survived throughout the region. The incorporation of Persia brought Persian cultural and intellectual traditions into Islamic civilisation, and they influenced Islamic statecraft, philosophy and literature for centuries. The Arab conquest of Spain in the 710s established Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula for nearly eight centuries. It created the civilisation of al-Andalus, whose philosophical, scientific and literary works later helped transmit Greek and Arabic learning to medieval Europe through Latin translation. Arabic spread as a language of government, commerce, religion and scholarship from Spain to Central Asia. Scholars across that whole distance could read one another, and Arabic became one of the great vehicles of pre-modern learning. Umayyad architecture, from the Dome of the Rock to the Great Mosque of Damascus, set models that later Islamic religious building followed. The establishment of Islam across the Middle East and North Africa was a consequence above all of the early Arab conquests, which the Umayyads consolidated and extended. It influenced the political, cultural and religious development of this region for the following thirteen centuries.
fields.decline: The Umayyad Caliphate fell in 750 CE. Its founding political choices had caused difficulties that accumulated over nearly a century, until they produced a revolutionary coalition too broad to suppress. The chief difficulty was that the dynasty stood for Arab tribal supremacy in an empire whose Muslim community was becoming increasingly non-Arab. As the number of mawali grew, particularly in Iraq, Persia and Central Asia, the gap between the egalitarian message of Islam and the hierarchical practice of Umayyad rule became intolerable. The Muslims of Khorasan, both mawali and settled Arab colonists, formed the social base of the Abbasid Revolution. The Shia, who had never accepted Umayyad legitimacy after Karbala, added their hostility to it. The great Berber Revolt in North Africa broke out in 739–740 over discriminatory taxation, demands for slaves and unequal treatment of Berber Muslims who had fought in the conquests. It showed that the periphery was prepared to contest Umayyad authority by force. The crisis deepened with the bitter rivalry between the Qays (northern Arab) and Yaman (Qahtan, or southern Arab) tribal factions. After the murder of al-Walid II in 744 the dynasty descended into the Third Fitna, which paralysed its armies just when unity was most needed. The Abbasid Revolution, proclaimed in Khorasan in 747 under Abu Muslim, moved west very quickly. In January 750 the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, was defeated at the Battle of the Great Zab, pursued into Egypt and killed. The Abbasids massacred most of the Umayyad family; the most famous survivor, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Spain and founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756. The new dynasty shifted the centre of the caliphate to Iraq, where al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762. Umayyad rule in the east was over and the Abbasid era had begun.
fields.summary: Within a single century the Umayyad Caliphate created one of the largest empires the world had yet seen. The expansion was rapid, and its religious and linguistic consequences lasted, so that it remains a founding political event of the Islamic world.
fields.teaser: Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyad Caliphate built one of the largest empires the world had yet seen, stretching from Spain to Central Asia and the Indus. It made Arabic the language of government and learning across that territory.
fields.t0: The Umayyads turned the caliphate into a hereditary monarchy ruled from Damascus, from 661 to 750.
fields.t1: Their conquests reached from Spain to Sind and Central Asia. They spread Arabic and prepared the ground for Islam across three continents.
fields.t2: Favouring Arabs over non-Arab converts bred revolt; the Abbasids overthrew them in 750, though a survivor founded a new Umayyad state in Spain.
fields.dyk: Abd al-Malik's gold dinar of 697 dropped Byzantine and Persian imagery for Arabic Quranic inscriptions, creating a distinctly Islamic coinage.
